title: Cross-fusedops Serialization & Stability Experiments
summary: Working notes and experiment log for randomized serialization of fused operators across FlashPaged and FlashAttention execution paths. Goal: reproduce intermittent regression that surfaces as 95th/99th latency spikes in mixed-sequence workloads and propose mitigations (serialization ordering, consumer backpressure, lightweight checksums).
content:
Purpose:
- Investigate stability regressions when the fused-op planner serializes multiple fused kernels into a single launch path (observed in mixed short+long sequence traffic).
- Determine whether serialization ordering or cross-kernel resource contention (shared scratchpads, tiling buffers) drives 95/99 latency tails.

Background/context:
- Repro trigger: production trace 2024-10-29 showing intermittent 10–30ms tail spikes on A100 fleets using FlashPaged + fused attention ops.
- Suspect interactions: fused_matmul+softmax fusion vs. paged-prefetch schedule causing warp thrashing.
- Related artifacts: PR 812 (runtime: fusedops-serializer), JIRA RUN-2418, kernel telemetry hooks (trace id + sensor id).

Experiments run (high-level):
1) Randomized serialization order sweep (local 1xA100): 1000 runs per seed, mix ratios short:long = 70:30. Measured p50/p95/p99 and kernel occupancy.
   - Command snippet: ./bench/runner --workload=mix --short_prob=0.7 --serialize_mode=random --seed=42 --traces=1000
   - Observation: rare ~0.8% runs produce p99 spikes ~3x baseline. Spikes correlate with single kernel launch that has >20% register spill.

2) Deterministic ordering (always short-first, always long-first): isolate whether order matters.
   - Short-first reduced spikes by ~60%. Long-first increased spike frequency.

3) Scratchpad aliasing probe: force separate scratch allocations per fusedop vs shared pool.
   - With dedicated scratch allocations, spike frequency drops to ~0.1%.

4) Prefetch timing offset test: shift paged prefetch by +/- 2ms relative to fused op launch.
   - Early prefetch (prefetch ahead) reduced spikes; late prefetch increased them. Hints at contention on memory bus during kernel handshake.

5) Microtrace sampling with event-level counters (SM utilization, warps_active, l2_bw): correlated high L2 BW bursts with spike runs.

Key findings / hypotheses:
- Primary hypothesis: serialization of fusedops can create temporal hot-spots on shared scratchpad regions and L2 bandwidth leading to kernel-level thrashing on certain launch orderings.
- Secondary hypothesis: kernel register pressure increases when a long sequence kernel follows a short sequence kernel due to allocator fragmentation, causing occasional spills and long latency.
- Prefetch timing is a reliable lever — moving paged prefetch earlier smooths the contention window.

Quantitative summary (representative numbers):
- Baseline (no serialization changes): p50=5.1ms, p95=9.8ms, p99=18.6ms
- Randomized serialization: p50=5.3ms, p95=10.4ms, p99=22.9ms (0.8% spike runs)
- Deterministic short-first: p50=5.2ms, p95=9.6ms, p99=11.5ms
- Dedicated scratchpads: p50=5.1ms, p95=9.2ms, p99=12.0ms
- Prefetch early: p50=5.0ms, p95=8.9ms, p99=10.8ms

Instrumentation notes:
- Added lightweight per-kernel checksum (64-bit xor of first/last tile) to detect cross-kernel memory corruption – no corruption observed, so root cause not silent memory races.
- Extended traces with "serializer_id" and "scratch_pool_id" to link launches to scratch allocation behavior.
- Capture config: perf counters: sm_efficiency, l2_read_bytes, l2_write_bytes, gld_ldst_64b, regs_spilled_from_block.

Edge cases observed:
- Multi-tenant small-batch coalescing sometimes coalesces a short sequence with a subsequent long sequence into a single fused schedule leading to the pathological ordering.
- When quantized kernels (int8) are in the mix, register pressure behavior changes and spikes are less reproducible — quantization changes allocator layout.

Mitigations tested (and their tradeoffs):
1) Prefer short-first serialization by default for mixed-batch coalescer.
   - Pros: reduces spikes significantly.
   - Cons: might slightly increase latency for long-only workloads (bench: +0.6ms p50).

2) Option: per-fusedop dedicated scratchpool allocation for high-risk stacks.
   - Pros: near elimination of spikes in tests.
   - Cons: increased memory usage on GPU (~3–8% per SM depending on tiling). Requires heuristics to enable only for stacks with high scatter.

3) Adaptive prefetch scheduler: detect high L2 BW and prefetch earlier.
   - Pros: non-invasive, relative small performance improvement.
   - Cons: complexity in runtime; needs robust thresholds to avoid thrash.

4) Lightweight serialization guard: if serializer detects a "dangerous" ordering (long after short, shared scratchpool), delay/fence the launch by a few microseconds to allow prefetch absorb.
   - Pros: reduces spikes without allocating extra scratch memory.
   - Cons: introduces added jitter; needs careful backpressure handling to avoid throughput loss.

Recommended short-term actions (next 2 weeks):
- Roll default to short-first serialization in staging for mixed workloads (ticket: RUN-2425).
- Add per-fusedop scratchpool flag behind a config (allow runtime to opt-in for problematic models).
- Add an A/B canary with adaptive prefetch schedule on one Dedicated cluster. Measure p99 over 48h.

Longer-term research directions:
- Explore a stochastic allocator that places long-sequence kernels onto separate register banks/scratch regions proactively.
- Model-aware planner: feed sequence-length distribution into the fusedop serializer so it can pick stable ordering heuristics.
- Investigate compiler-level tiling changes to reduce inter-kernel L2 bursts (coordinate with research group).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why do quantized kernels sometimes avoid the spike? Is it due to different register pressure patterns or scheduling differences? Need controlled microbench for quant vs fp16 stacks.
- Are there cross-VM or driver-level interactions (NCCL/driver queue) contributing? Need to run same workload on bare metal vs container shim.

Action items (owners):
- RUN-2425: short-first default rollout (owner: Rafael Ortiz) — due 2024-12-10.
- RUN-2431: per-fusedop scratchpool config + perf test (owner: Priya Nair) — due 2024-12-18.
- RUN-2432: canary adaptive prefetch + 48h measurement on dedicated cluster (owner: Anika Gupta) — due 2024-12-20.

Notes to self / informal thoughts:
- Keep kernel checksum cheap; can remove later. Good for early detection but adds tiny overheads.
- When writing canary, add debug sampling only on 0.1% of requests to avoid telemetry explosion.
- Talk to console team about surfacing scratchpool pressure in route dashboards (help SREs triage).

Appendix: quick repro steps (dev machine):
1) git checkout pr/812 && cargo build --release
2) ./bench/runner --workload=mix --short_prob=0.7 --serialize_mode=random --seed=7 --traces=2000 --telemetry=mini
3) tail -f /tmp/bench-traces | jq '. | select(.p99_spike==true)'

Slack threads and references:
- #runtime-kernels thread: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C02RUNTIME/p1711754000000000
- Related confluence: ServingRuntime/Kernel-Serialization-Notes (internal)

If you have time, please review the proposed short-first rollout plan and the scratchpool opt-in API shape (sketch below):
- API: fusedop::Scheduler::set_scratchpool_policy("per-op" | "shared" | "auto")
- Default for now: "auto" -> short-first heuristic enabled

End of notes.
